Article.ArticleTitle: Longitudinal Changes in Exocrine Biomarkers in Children at Risk of Type 1 Diabetes in the ENDIA Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: The exocrine pancreas is increasingly implicated in type 1 diabetes. Noninvasive biomarkers of exocrine function, fecal elastase-1 (FE-1) and serum immunoreactive trypsin (IRT), may provide early insight into disease pathogenesis. We investigated the temporal relationship between exocrine biomarkers and type 1 diabetes development in children.

FE-1 and IRT concentrations were measured prospectively in 301 at-risk children followed in the Environmental Determinants of Islet Autoimmunity (ENDIA) cohort from birth. A total of 216 children provided 1,679 stool samples; 242 provided 1,014 serum samples. Biomarker trajectories were compared between children who developed islet autoimmunity or type 1 diabetes and age- and sex-matched control children negative for autoantibodies in a nested case-control design. Adjusted linear mixed models were used.

Two biomarker patterns were observed. FE-1 concentrations were lower during the first 6 months of life in children who subsequently developed multiple islet autoantibodies or type 1 diabetes (β-coefficient at birth -0.61 [95% CI -1.04, -0.17]; P = 0.006; β-coefficient at 3 months -0.39 [95% CI -0.69, -0.09]; P = 0.010); IRT concentrations were lower in children who developed type 1 diabetes 12 months (β = -0.30 [95% CI -0.58, -0.02]; P = 0.034) and 18 months (β = -0.40 [95% CI -0.71, -0.10]; P = 0.008) before type 1 diabetes diagnosis.

Changes in exocrine biomarkers were detectable early in the natural history of type 1 diabetes, with a delayed rise of FE-1 in infants who later progressed to multiple islet autoantibodies or type 1 diabetes and a decrease in IRT following islet autoantibody seroconversion.

Article.ArticleTitle: Gout as a risk factor for lower-extremity amputation in diabetes: a nationwide, register-based case-control study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Non-healing diabetic foot ulcers are a major precursor to lower-extremity amputation (LEA) in diabetes, and gout may be an overlooked contributor. We hypothesised that individuals with both diabetes and gout have a higher risk of LEA than those with diabetes alone, with the strongest effect at more distal amputation levels.

In a nationwide case-control study of 601,541 individuals with type 2 diabetes, we identified 4912 cases with LEA and 39,101 age- and sex-matched control participants. Gout exposure was determined using ICD-10 diagnoses and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical codes for urate-lowering therapy. Associations were estimated using conditional logistic regression, adjusting for diabetes duration, peripheral arterial disease, acute myocardial infarction and late diabetes complications.

Gout was associated with an increased risk of LEA (OR 1.85, 95% CI 1.69, 2.02) in unadjusted analyses, and the association remained significant after full adjustment (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.37, 1.69). A significant trend (p=0.03) was observed across amputation levels, with potentially higher risk at more anatomically distal sites although no statistically significant differences were observed between individual amputation levels: OR 1.37 (95% CI 1.12, 1.68) for above-knee amputations, increasing to OR 1.65 (95% CI 1.32, 2.05) for toe amputations.

Co-existing gout is an independent risk factor for LEA in individuals with type 2 diabetes. The risk is elevated across all amputation levels, with the most pronounced effect potentially being at distal anatomical sites. These findings highlight the need for increased awareness of gout when managing individuals with type 2 diabetes at risk of LEA.

Article.ArticleTitle: Presentation, management, and outcomes of ectopic Cushing syndrome: an international, multicentre, retrospective, cohort study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Ectopic Cushing syndrome is a rare condition with scarce outcome data. We sought to characterise its course and determinants of complications and mortality.

In this international, multicentre, retrospective, cohort study, 49 high-volume endocrine referral centres across Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and New Zealand identified consecutive eligible patients. We included patients with a clinical diagnosis of ectopic Cushing syndrome, defined by expert adjudication at the treating institution with at least one of the following criteria: inferior petrosal sinus sampling or dynamic testing supportive of ectopic Cushing syndrome, biochemical remission of hypercortisolism following treatment of the ectopic Cushing syndrome source (surgical excision, radiotherapy, or cryoablation), evidence of a non-metastatic tumoural source of ectopic Cushing syndrome, either on initial or subsequent imaging, or evidence of a metastatic tumoural source of ectopic Cushing syndrome either on imaging or from chart notes. Data collection was completed between May 31, 2024 and April 22, 2025. Clinical features, biochemical severity, management, complications, and mortality were assessed. The primary outcome was Cushing syndrome-related mortality (investigator-adjudicated). Secondary outcomes were overall mortality and incidence of complications. Outcomes were stratified based on biochemical remission and timeline since diagnosis. Early (within 6 months of diagnosis) and late (>6 months after diagnosis) outcomes were analysed using landmark methods.

Among 1463 patients (median age 51 years [IQR 37-64; range 3-87], 824 [56·3%] women, 639 [43·7%] men, and 1021 [69·8%] of White race), 836 (57·1%) had metastatic disease. Severe hypercortisolism (1204 [91·1%] of 1321) and hypokalaemia (1111 [79·4%] of 1399) were common. Median duration of follow-up was 57 months (IQR 19-124). Cushing syndrome-related death occurred in 196 (13·4%) patients. 626 (42·8%) patients died overall. Infection occurred in 464 (31·7%) patients, venous thromboembolism in 124 (8·5%), cardiovascular events in 93 (6·4%), and cerebrovascular events in 37 (2·5%). Achievement of complete biochemical remission within 6 months of diagnosis was independently associated with lower risk of late complications (adjusted HR 0·55 [95% CI 0·38-0·80]) and Cushing syndrome-related mortality (0·49 [0·27-0·89]), whereas no association was observed with non-Cushing syndrome-related mortality.

Outcomes in ectopic Cushing syndrome are driven by early control of hypercortisolism. Failure to achieve remission within 6 months is associated with markedly worse complications and mortality, supporting ectopic Cushing syndrome as a time-critical endocrine emergency.

Article.ArticleTitle: Genetic subtyping of MASLD reveals a glucose-lowering axis linked to GCKR alternative splicing.

Abstract.AbstractText: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a global metabolic condition with a complex relationship to type 2 diabetes. Yet human genetic studies suggest the existence of a MASLD subtype with favourable glycaemic effects, raising a clinically important question: how can hepatic steatosis coexist with improved glycaemic outcomes? We aimed to determine whether MASLD comprises genetically distinct subtypes with divergent glycaemic consequences, and to define the genetic basis of a glucose-lowering MASLD subtype.

We integrated genetic and triglyceride-related metabolomic profiles to cluster 18 established MASLD-associated variants and construct mutually adjusted partitioned polygenic risk scores (PRSs) in the UK Biobank. We tested associations with hepatic biomarkers, liver outcomes and type 2 diabetes, and replicated glycaemic findings in an independent Chinese cohort (the Taizhou Longitudinal Study [TZL]). We prioritised candidate loci using colocalisation and fine-mapping and performed allele-specific functional assays and structural modelling to investigate the underlying mechanism at the lead locus.

Partitioned PRSs revealed bidirectional glycaemic axes: one PRS lowered fasting glucose and type 2 diabetes risk, whereas the remaining PRSs increased both, despite all associating with higher liver injury markers and adverse liver outcomes. The divergent glycaemic effects were replicated in the TZL. To pinpoint the genetic basis of the glucose-lowering axis, colocalisation and fine-mapping prioritised GCKR rs1260326 (C>T) as a shared MASLD-type 2 diabetes signal and the lead cis-pQTL for circulating glucokinase regulatory protein (GKRP). Functional experiments showed that the rs1260326 T allele promotes exon-15 skipping in GCKR, reduces the abundance of full-length GKRP and yields a truncated protein. In silico structural modelling suggested that the truncated GKRP isoform may have reduced binding affinity for glucokinase, although this predicted effect requires experimental validation.

MASLD comprises genetically distinct subtypes with opposing glycaemic and type 2 diabetes risk profiles. Within the glucose-lowering subtype, rs1260326-mediated alternative splicing of GCKR provides a potential mechanistic link to reduced GKRP abundance and glycaemic protection. These findings support a more granular view of MASLD heterogeneity and may inform future subtype-specific risk stratification and prevention.

Article.ArticleTitle: Common Genetic Variants Near SLC2A2 and Glycemic Response to Glimepiride in the GRADE Comparative Effectiveness Clinical Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Optimizing second-line therapy for type 2 diabetes remains challenging because of interindividual variability in response. Current treatment selection does not consider personal genetic profiles. To address this gap, we conducted a pharmacogenomic genome-wide association study (GWAS) in a randomized comparative effectiveness trial to identify genetic predictors of glycemic response to insulin glargine, glimepiride, liraglutide, and sitagliptin when added to metformin.

In the Glycemia Reduction Approaches in Type 2 Diabetes: A Comparative Effectiveness Study (GRADE), we performed a GWAS for the time to reach primary (glycated hemoglobin [HbA1c] ≥7%) and secondary (HbA1c >7.5%) metabolic failure. We conducted replication in independent cohorts, performed fine mapping of the top variants near SLC2A2, evaluated them for physiologic impact using oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT) and response to acute glipizide challenge, and characterized glycemic response to glimepiride in an slc2a2-mutated zebrafish model.

rs2129019 in SLC2A2 encoding GLUT2 was enriched in African/African American participants and conferred a 38% increased risk of metabolic failure per A allele on glimepiride (P = 1.55 × 10-8). Carriers had impaired β-cell function, evidenced by a lower C-peptide index during OGTT, and diminished glucose-lowering response to acute sulfonylurea challenge. Genetic manipulation in zebrafish confirmed that slc2a2 disruption attenuated the glucose-lowering effect of glimepiride.

Genetic variation influences glycemic response to glucose-lowering medications, with SLC2A2 emerging as a genetic factor that modulates sulfonylurea response. These findings warrant further study to evaluate whether low-response allele carriers would benefit from alternative glucose-lowering therapies to advance precision diabetes care.

Article.ArticleTitle: Real-world evidence for decisions in diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Randomised controlled trials underpin the evidence base for diabetes interventions but have important limitations, including being conducted in selective populations, with restricted follow-up times and treatment pathways that differ from routine clinical practice. Real-world data (RWD) offer an opportunity to address questions beyond the scope of trials, including the comparative effectiveness of interventions, assessment of longer-term outcomes, and treatment effects in under-represented populations. However, the credibility of real-world evidence (RWE) varies widely due to data quality and methodological challenges. The REDDIE (Real-world Evidence for Decisions in Diabetes) programme examined how RWD can generate robust, decision-relevant evidence for diabetes by analysing multiple national registries, evaluating regulatory expectations and conducting target trial emulations of landmark studies. Evidence from REDDIE and the wider literature demonstrates that well-designed observational analyses can replicate major trial findings and extend evidence to broader populations. However, credibility critically depends on careful alignment between the research question, database fitness, study design and analytical methods. Target trial emulation and modern causal inference approaches can mitigate key biases but cannot overcome fundamental limitations of routine data, including unmeasured confounding and incomplete variable capture. RWE and RCTs should be viewed as complementary sources of evidence. We outline a practical framework for the design, analysis and interpretation of RWE studies in diabetes to support more robust and decision-relevant use of RWD by regulators, health technology assessment agencies and clinicians.

Article.ArticleTitle: Associations of long-term exposure to air pollution with glucose homeostasis biomarkers and diabetes-related comorbidities in people with recent-onset type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Air pollution (AP) contributes to diabetes progression and comorbidities, but underlying mechanisms remain unclear, as no observational studies have applied gold-standard phenotyping or distinguished between the effects of type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes and diabetes subtypes. We examined whether AP exposure was associated with glucose homeostasis biomarkers and diabetes-related comorbidities in people with recent-onset type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes and diabetes subtypes.

This cross-sectional analysis is based on data from 1120 participants in the German Diabetes Study (417 with type 1 diabetes and 703 with type 2 diabetes). The glucose homeostasis biomarkers used were HbA1c, insulin sensitivity (clamp-derived M value), insulin secretion (glucagon-stimulated C-peptide6min) and insulin clearance (clamp derived). Diabetes-related comorbidities included CVD risk (SCORE2-Diabetes), V ˙ O 2 max as an indicator of cardiorespiratory fitness, albuminuria as a marker of kidney function and the presence of distal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (DSPN). Five-year means of exposure to AP (particulate matter [PM] with diameters of <2.5 μm [PM2.5] and <10 μm [PM10] and nitrogen dioxide [NO2] before baseline at individual residential addresses were examined. Associations between each exposure-outcome pair were estimated per 1 IQR increase in air pollutants using multivariable linear and logistic regression. Two-pollutant analysis, cumulative risk index (CRI) analysis and insulin-treated type 1 diabetes model analysis were performed as sensitivity analyses.

Among those with type 1 diabetes, higher PM2.5 was associated with higher HbA1c (exp[β]=1.07 [95% CI 1.03, 1.11]), insulin secretion (exp[β]=1.19 [95% CI 1.03, 1.36]), lower V ˙ O 2 max (exp[β]=0.94 [95% CI 0.89, 0.99]) and higher albuminuria (exp[β]=1.72 [95% CI 1.34, 2.20]). Among type 2 diabetes, higher PM2.5 was associated with higher HbA1c (exp[β]=1.04 [95% CI 1.01, 1.06]), lower insulin sensitivity (β=-0.42 [95% CI -0.82, -0.03]), lower insulin secretion (exp[β]=0.94 [95% CI 0.89, 0.99]), lower insulin clearance (exp[β]=0.92 [95% CI 0.87, 0.98]), higher CVD risk (exp[β]=1.07 [95% CI 0.99, 1.16]), lower V ˙ O 2 max (exp[β]=0.91 [95% CI 0.88, 0.95]), higher albuminuria (exp[β]=1.71 [95% CI 1.41, 2.08]) and higher odds of DSPN (OR 1.53 [95% CI 1.02, 2.32]). Similar associations were observed for PM10 and NO2. Associations were directionally attenuated in two-pollutant models but remained consistent in CRI and insulin-treated type 1 diabetes analyses. Differences were observed in associations between diabetes subtypes.

Long-term AP exposure was consistently associated with higher HbA1c; reduced whole-body insulin sensitivity, secretion and clearance; and an increased burden of diabetes-related comorbidities in type 2 diabetes. Associations were less consistent in type 1 diabetes. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01055093.

Article.ArticleTitle: Pregestational maternal diabetes primes neonatal beta cell dysfunction with structural remodelling, impaired calcium buffering and altered mTORC2-Gαq-PKCα signalling in a pig model.

Abstract.AbstractText: Offspring of mothers with diabetes are at increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes, and this predisposition is established during fetal life. The aim of this study was to define the functional, morphological and molecular alterations in neonatal pancreatic islets associated with maternal hyperglycaemia, with a particular focus on beta cells, an area that remains poorly understood. Given its similarity to humans in endocrine pancreas development, the pig was used as a translational animal model.

Using genetically diabetic and beta cell reporter pig models, we performed functional assessments of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in vivo and in situ using fresh pancreatic tissue slices from neonatal piglets born to hyperglycaemic mothers (PHGs) or normoglycaemic mothers (PNGs). Morphological and molecular profiling, including proteomics and single-cell RNA-seq, were performed to elucidate molecular changes reflecting the developmental impact of maternal diabetes on offspring metabolic health, with a particular focus on neonatal beta cells.

PHGs were born hyperglycaemic, hyperinsulinaemic and insulin resistant, exhibiting markedly delayed glucose and insulin response curves following oral glucose administration, with more pronounced effects in male piglets. Elevated basal insulin secretion and an almost blunted glucose responsiveness of pancreatic tissue slices were associated with increased insulin and somatostatin content, expansion of beta (+35%) and delta (+47%) cell populations, and organisation into larger islet clusters. Neonatal PHG islets exhibited a molecular profile consistent with intrinsic beta cell dysfunction that partially overlapped with type 2 diabetes (e.g. RBP4 upregulation), together with alterations in glucose sensing (near absence of GLUT2), nutrient metabolism resembling congenital hyperinsulinism (HADH downregulation), and cytosolic Ca2⁺ homeostasis (near absence of the Ca2⁺ buffer calbindin D28K). In addition to an ATF4-dominated stress signature, a shift towards a distinct PHG beta cell subcluster characterised by low expression of ribosomal genes was observed, with an adaptive early-response-gene-mediated transcriptional reactivity. In contrast to the Gαs-adenylyl cyclase-cAMP-PKA signalling axis that dominated in PNG beta cells, neonatal PHG beta cells displayed distinct alterations in Gαq-PLC-PKCα signalling components, the mTORC2 target PKCα, and CREB1, suggesting a restructured signalling architecture.

Our findings reveal altered islet modelling with a unique beta cell dysfunction profile that partially overlaps with, but differs from, that of type 2 diabetes. A shift towards a beta cell subcluster exhibiting an adaptive early-response-gene-mediated transcriptional reactivity and an ATF4-associated transcriptional stress signature provides insight into molecular alterations associated with fetal exposure to maternal diabetes and may contribute to the increased risk of metabolic disease in offspring.

Article.ArticleTitle: Cotransplantation With Human AAT-MSCs Enhances Human Islet Graft Survival in Humanized Mice by Modulating B- and T-Cell Responses.

Abstract.AbstractText: Immune-mediated rejection remains a major barrier to long-term success of islet/stem cell-derived islet transplantation for type 1 diabetes. We evaluated whether cotransplantation of human islets with human α-1 antitrypsin-overexpressing mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (AAT-MSCs) improves islet graft survival by modulating human immune responses in a humanized diabetic mouse model. Humanized NOD/SCID/IL2Rγ-/- (NSG) mice were generated by irradiation and transfer of human CD34+ hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, resulting in stable T- and B-cell reconstitution. Diabetes was induced by multiple doses of low-dose streptozotocin (STZ), after which mice received intrahepatic transplants of human islets alone or together with AAT-MSCs and were monitored for 100 days. Cotransplantation with AAT-MSCs markedly improved glycemic control, prolonged graft survival, and reduced the risk of rejection. These beneficial effects were associated with lower serum IgM levels, which inversely correlated with graft rejection, and with expansion of regulatory B cells (Bregs), followed by durable suppression of T helper 1, T helper 17, and cytotoxic T cell responses. Cotransplant grafts showed improved insulin preservation and enrichment of interleukin (IL) 10+ cells within islets. In vitro, AAT-MSCs promoted Breg differentiation, shifted cytokine production toward IL-10 over IL-6, and attenuated activated B cell-mediated cytotoxicity against human islets. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AAT-MSC cotransplantation promotes immune tolerance and human islet graft function, supporting its translational potential to reduce reliance on systemic immunosuppression in the clinic.

Immune-mediated rejection limits the long-term success of islet and stem cell-derived islet transplantation in type 1 diabetes, and strategies that protect the graft without systemic immunosuppression are needed. We asked whether cotransplanting human islets with α-1 antitrypsin-overexpressing mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (AAT-MSCs) improves graft outcomes in humanized mice, and how human immune responses are affected. AAT-MSC cotransplantation improved glycemic control, prolonged graft survival, and shifted immune responses toward a more regulatory, less inflammatory profile. These findings support further development of AAT-MSCs as an adjunct to reduce reliance on systemic immunosuppression in islet transplantation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Transient Cognitive Vulnerability After Hypoglycemia in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: Evidence From Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Cognitive Ecologic Momentary Assessment.

Abstract.AbstractText: Adults with type 1 diabetes experience short-term changes in cognitive performance after glycemic events; however, the duration of such cognitive effects remains unclear. We examined whether hypoglycemic and hyperglycemic events and rapid glucose changes were associated with changes in processing speed or sustained attention in adults with type 1 diabetes and whether these associations varied by time since the event.

Participants (N = 190) completed 15 days of smartphone-based ecologic momentary assessment (EMA; 3 prompts/day) paired with continuous glucose monitoring. Cognitive performance (median reaction time and accuracy) was tested using digit symbol matching (DSM) and gradual-onset continuous performance testing (GCPT; sustained attention) by TestMyBrain (processing speed). Glycemic exposures were defined as hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia lasting ≥15 min and rapid (5-min) increases or decreases in glucose >15 mg/dL, occurring during nonoverlapping intervals: 0-1, 1-2, and 2-3 h before EMA. Multilevel models estimated associations between glycemic exposures and cognitive performance, adjusting for age, EMA count, and interruptions.

Hypoglycemic events occurring within 0-1 h of EMA were associated with slower reaction time and poorer performance on DSM and GCPT. No associations were observed for events occurring 1-2 or 2-3 h before EMA. Hyperglycemic events and rapid glucose increases or decreases were not associated with cognition across most outcomes or time windows.

Hypoglycemia was associated with a transient period of cognitive vulnerability largely confined to the hour after an event, with little evidence of delayed effects. Findings support avoiding or exercising caution during cognitively demanding tasks for up to an hour after a hypoglycemic event.

Article.ArticleTitle: Clinical Guidance for Disease-Modifying Immunotherapy in Children and Adolescents With New-Onset (Stage 3) Type 1 Diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: The 2026 U.S. approval of teplizumab, for children and adolescents aged 8-17 years with recently diagnosed stage 3 type 1 diabetes, changes the first weeks after diagnosis. Clinicians must treat hyperglycemia and teach lifelong care skills while considering whether to preserve residual β-cell function. Teplizumab is the current clinical exemplar, although the implementation challenges extend beyond one agent. This article addresses who should lead care, how to approach eligibility and timing, how to assess β-cell reserve and infection risk, how to sequence treatment with diabetic ketoacidosis recovery and early education, and how to monitor treatment safely. Teplizumab-specific recommendations are identified, with broader principles framed for adaptation across health systems.

Article.ArticleTitle: Fetal, placental and amniotic fluid volume across gestation in women with type 1 diabetes: a prospective MRI study.

Abstract.AbstractText: The aim of this study was to compare fetal, placental and amniotic fluid volumes across gestation by use of MRI in women with type 1 diabetes and women without diabetes.

This prospective longitudinal cohort study is part of the FaPDi cohort study. The study included pregnant women with type 1 diabetes and women without diabetes who gave birth at Aalborg University Hospital between November 2020 and April 2023. All participants were invited for MRI scans at 15-20, 26-30 and 34-38 weeks' gestation, from which fetal, placental and amniotic fluid volumes were obtained. The groups were compared across gestation using multiple linear regressions and mixed-effects models.

A total of 63 pregnant women were included in the analysis (25 with type 1 diabetes and 38 without diabetes). In women with type 1 diabetes, the fetal, placental and amniotic volumes were significantly increased at visits 2 and 3. At visit 3, the adjusted differences between groups were 385.9 cm3 (95% CI 140.9, 631.0; p<0.01), 187.8 cm3 (95% CI 35.4, 340.3; p=0.02) and 420.4 cm3 (95% CI 19.5, 821.2; p=0.04) for the fetal, placental and amniotic volumes, respectively. Placental weight to birthweight ratio was increased at delivery among women with type 1 diabetes (p<0.01), but no differences in the intrauterine volume ratios were observed. Maternal HbA1c showed a positive linear correlation with all volumes at visits 2 and 3, with the strongest correlations shown for amniotic fluid volume (R2=0.36).

MRI provides a unique insight into the intrauterine consequences of type 1 diabetes. Pregnancies complicated by type 1 diabetes are characterised by increased fetal, placental and amniotic fluid volumes. The strong association between maternal HbA1c and amniotic fluid volume suggests that amniotic fluid dynamics may provide additional insight into the intrauterine consequences of maternal glucose regulation.

Article.ArticleTitle: It's All One Trial: a continuous master-protocol framework to accelerate development and confirmation of disease-modifying therapies for type 1 diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: The time required for clinical development and regulatory approval of disease-modifying therapies for type 1 diabetes is the longest of any therapeutic area. Teplizumab, the only product that has received an accelerated approval in the USA for people with stage 3 type 1 diabetes, will require about a decade for its Phase III and confirmatory trial to be completed and full approval to be achieved. This article proposes the 'It's All One Trial' (OT) framework, a single master protocol with one continuously randomised population, one prospective statistical structure, and uninterrupted follow-up spanning early investigation, accelerated approval based on an intermediate endpoint, and later confirmation of durability and clinical benefit. The OT framework is compared with current clinical development practices for treatments aimed at preserving insulin secretion in people with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. Teplizumab's Phase III PROTECT trial and confirmatory βETA PRESERVE trials provide observed and projected timelines for late-stage development. Based on prevailing early clinical development practices and observed and projected timelines of the teplizumab trials, the OT model could reduce total development time by approximately 45 months while increasing use of participant data and reducing the need for repeated enrolment, site activation and study restarts. Implementing the OT model could shorten development timelines, lower capital barriers, conserve scarce clinical trial resources and better honour patient participation by maintaining continuous randomised follow-up, protocol-directed care and a more direct path from early biological effect to durable evidence for practice and regulation.

Efficacy and safety of co-administered cagrilintide-semaglutide (CagriSema) 1·7 mg each and 1·0 mg each in adults with overweight or obesity (REDEFINE 9): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind within-dose-level, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 3b trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Cagrilintide-semaglutide (CagriSema) 2·4 mg each has shown clinically meaningful bodyweight reductions in global phase 3 studies. Different dosing options might support individual treatment responses and tolerability. We aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of once per week subcutaneous cagrilintide-semaglutide 1·7 mg each or 1·0 mg each versus placebo in participants with obesity or overweight and at least one obesity-related complication.

This multicentre, randomised, double-blind within-dose-level, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 3b trial (REDEFINE 9) was conducted across 24 sites in Canada, France, Germany, the UK, and the USA. Eligible participants were adults aged 18 years or older; with a BMI of at least 30 kg/m2 or at least 27 kg/m2 and one or more obesity-related complication; and without diabetes. Participants were randomly assigned (2:1:2:1) centrally, using block randomisation (block size of six) and a web-based system, to receive cagrilintide 1·7 mg plus semaglutide 1·7 mg (hereafter cagrilintide-semaglutide 1·7 mg each, starting at 0·25 mg each and escalated over 12 weeks), placebo 1·7 mg plus 1·7 mg (hereafter placebo 1·7 mg each), cagrilintide 1·0 mg plus semaglutide 1·0 mg (hereafter cagrilintide-semaglutide 1·0 mg each, starting at 0·25 mg each and escalated over 8 weeks), or placebo 1·0 mg plus 1·0 mg (hereafter placebo 1·0 mg each) for 68 weeks, plus nutrition and physical activity counselling until week 74. All treatments were administered subcutaneously once per week. The coprimary endpoints were relative mean change in bodyweight from baseline to week 68 and proportion of participants reaching a bodyweight reduction of at least 5% at week 68, assessed in the full analysis set (defined as all randomly assigned participants). Safety was assessed in the safety analysis set (defined as all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of the study drug). This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06388187 (completed).

From June 24 to Oct 30, 2024, 333 participants were assessed for eligibility and 24 were excluded. 309 participants were randomly assigned (full analysis set: 104 assigned to cagrilintide-semaglutide 1·7 mg each, 103 to cagrilintide-semaglutide 1·0 mg each, and 102 to pooled placebo). 308 participants received at least one dose of the study drug. 291 (94%) of 309 participants completed the study and 254 (82%) were on treatment at week 68. The mean age was 48·0 years (SD 13·6) and mean BMI was 39·1 kg/m2 (6·8). 239 (77%) participants were female, and 70 (23%) were male. For the efficacy estimand, the mean relative change from baseline in bodyweight at week 68 was -20·7% (SE 0·9) with cagrilintide-semaglutide 1·7 mg each, -21·0% (1·0) with cagrilintide-semaglutide 1·0 mg each, and -2·0% (1·0) with the pooled placebo. Bodyweight reductions were significantly greater with both doses of cagrilintide-semaglutide than with placebo (estimated treatment difference [ETD] -18·8 percentage points [95% CI -21·5 to -16·0]; p<0·0001 for the 1·7 mg each dose and -19·0 percentage points [-21·8 to -16·2]; p<0·0001 for the 1·0 mg each dose). The proportion of participants reaching bodyweight reductions of at least 5% at week 68 was significantly greater with cagrilintide-semaglutide than with placebo (95·1% [SE 2·7] with the 1·7 mg each dose vs 33·4% [5·6] with placebo, ETD 61·7 percentage points [95% CI 49·5-74·0], p<0·0001; and 96·3% [2·2] with the 1·0 mg each dose, ETD 63·0 percentage points [51·1-74·9], p<0·0001). Adverse events were reported in 102 (99%) of 103 participants receiving cagrilintide-semaglutide 1·7 mg each, 98 (95%) of 103 receiving cagrilintide-semaglutide 1·0 mg each, and 93 (91%) of 102 receiving the placebo. Most adverse events were mild or moderate and gastrointestinal-related. No deaths were reported.

Cagrilintide-semaglutide at 1·7 mg each and 1·0 mg each was superior to placebo at reducing bodyweight in adults with overweight or obesity, suggesting that different dose levels might support treatment flexibility.

Article.ArticleTitle: Should continuous glucose monitoring redefine prediabetes?

Abstract.AbstractText: Prediabetes is a clinically useful but biologically heterogeneous risk state defined by episodic laboratory thresholds that identify overlapping rather than identical populations. Continuous glucose monitoring can reveal temporal glycaemic variation that fasting plasma glucose, OGTT and HbA1c cannot capture. Recent evidence indicates that sensor-derived metrics distinguish conventionally defined prediabetes from normoglycaemia and can stratify future glycaemic risk, making eventual incorporation into classification scientifically plausible. The case for immediate diagnostic use, however, is not established. Continuous glucose monitoring measures interstitial rather than venous plasma glucose; device performance and sampling duration influence the derived metrics; and treatment-oriented glucose targets were not developed as diagnostic cut-offs in people without diabetes. Before a continuous glucose monitoring phenotype can be incorporated into the definition of prediabetes, it should demonstrate reproducibility over time and across devices, provide clinically meaningful information beyond established tests and risk factors, change a management decision and show a favourable downstream balance between benefit and harm. Until these conditions are met, continuous glucose monitoring is better positioned as an instrument for phenotyping and risk stratification than as an independent diagnostic criterion.

Article.ArticleTitle: Smart insulin pens with integrated bolus calculator vs tracking-only connected insulin pens in adults with diabetes on multiple daily injections: a multicentre randomised controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Connected insulin pens (CIPs) have emerged as a promising tool for diabetes management with multiple daily injections (MDI), but evidence supporting the incremental benefit of integrated bolus calculator functionality (smart insulin pens [SIPs]) over tracking-only CIPs remains lacking. We evaluated the efficacy and safety of SIPs with bolus calculator compared with tracking-only CIPs in adults with diabetes on MDI. We hypothesised that SIPs with bolus calculator would improve glycaemic management compared with tracking-only CIPs.

In this multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial conducted at nine medical centres in South Korea, we recruited adults aged 19-74 years with type 1 or type 2 diabetes on MDI therapy. Participants with HbA1c 58-108 mmol/mol (7.5-12.0%) were randomly assigned (1:1) using computer-generated block randomisation stratified by diabetes type (sequence generated by an independent statistician) to SIP with bolus calculator or tracking-only CIP for 12 weeks. All participants used continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). The primary outcome was the change in HbA1c from baseline to week 12. Secondary outcomes included CGM metrics, insulin dosing behaviour and safety.

A total of 120 participants were randomised to the SIP group (n=60) or the tracking-only CIP group (n=60); their mean (SD) age was 50.8 (14.8) years, 53 (44.2%) had type 1 diabetes and mean (SD) HbA1c was 69 (12) mmol/mol (8.5% [1.1%]). Of these, 116 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. HbA1c decreased more with SIP than with tracking-only CIP (adjusted mean difference -3.39 mmol/mol [-0.31%]; 95% CI -6.45, -0.22 mmol/mol [-0.59%, -0.02%]; p=0.036). Time in range (3.9-10.0 mmol/l) improved significantly with SIP (57.2% vs 50.8%; adjusted mean difference 6.58%; 95% CI 1.52%, 11.64%; p=0.012). SIP users had fewer missed bolus doses (3.4 vs 3.7 times/day; p=0.020) and higher bolus frequency (3.2 vs 2.8 times/day; p=0.011). No severe hypoglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in either group.

In this randomised controlled trial of adults with suboptimally controlled diabetes on MDI, SIP with bolus calculator significantly improved glycaemic management and dosing behaviour compared with tracking-only CIP.

Article.ArticleTitle: Dual stimulation of Wnt and IFN-γ pathways in human bone marrow-derived multipotent stromal cells produces an activated secretome that modulates autoimmune diabetes in NOD mice.

Abstract.AbstractText: Type 1 diabetes is characterised by continual autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells for which no curative therapy exists. We and others have demonstrated that the paracrine secretome of human multipotent stromal cells (MSCs) can induce islet regeneration and immune modulation; however, whether these effects persist in the context of ongoing autoimmunity remains unknown. Herein, we hypothesised that pharmacological licensing of MSCs with CHIR99021 and/or IFN-γ will generate conditioned media (CdM) with complementary regenerative and immunomodulatory properties. We also aimed to assess the modulation of autoimmune diabetes progression by licensed MSC CdM after intrapancreatic injection in NOD mice.

Human bone marrow-derived MSCs were licensed with CHIR99021, IFN-γ or a combination of both, for 24 h, to generate concentrated CHIR, IFN-γ or COMBO CdM, for intrapancreatic (iPan) injection into female NOD mice and for label-free MS-based secretome analyses. Short- and long-term glycaemic outcomes were assessed across type 1 diabetes recovery and prevention paradigms. Pancreas and spleen tissue were collected for tissue analyses to assess beta cell content and immune cell composition.

iPan injection of COMBO CdM immediately after hyperglycaemia onset in NOD mice transiently paused glycaemic elevation (mean ± SEM: 17 ± 3 vs 29 ± 2 mmol/l in basal media-injected controls), reduced severe insulitis and culminated in prolonged survival (mean ± SEM: 32 ± 2 days) compared with basal media-injected controls (mean ± SEM: 21 ± 3 days). In type 1 diabetes prevention experiments, COMBO CdM injection at 12 weeks of age expanded FoxP3+ Treg populations in the spleen and pancreas, and delayed hyperglycaemia onset by 4 weeks (mean ± SEM: 21 ± 0.9 vs 17 ± 0.4 weeks in basal media-injected mice). Early intervention in 8-week-old mice prior to signs of insulitis demonstrated that all CdM preparations preserved glucose tolerance, while CHIR CdM also increased beta cell mass. Proteomic profiling of COMBO CdM revealed unique upregulation of tolerogenic effectors including CD274/PD-L1, CCL7 and IDO1, alongside tissue reparative proteins including MET and TYMP, and proteins involved in extracellular matrix remodelling such as CTSB, CTSS and CTSL, providing a molecular basis for superior outcomes in vivo.

Combined pharmacological licensing of MSCs produces a biologically unique secretome with complementary regenerative and immunomodulatory properties that modulates autoimmune diabetes progression in NOD mice. These findings position MSC licensing and/or MSC CdM as an emerging therapeutic modality for the prevention of autoimmune destruction and regenerative medicine therapies for type 1 diabetes.

Article.ArticleTitle: Triphasic decline in kidney function after islet transplantation: sex-based differences and the impact of calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppression in a 20 year single-centre cohort.

Abstract.AbstractText: Islet transplantation alone (ITA) is an established treatment for severe hypoglycaemia in type 1 diabetes, requiring calcineurin inhibitor-based immunosuppression, which is associated with nephrotoxicity. These limitations have driven longstanding interest in calcineurin inhibitor-free strategies, which are now entering clinical translation. The aim of this study was to evaluate long-term kidney function in 223 adults (41% male) undergoing ITA at the University of Alberta Hospital (1999-2018) using eGFR.

Mixed-effects models were used to assess eGFR decline rates (ml min-1 1.73 m-2 per year) stratified by sex and baseline eGFR. Acute eGFR changes were assessed within 3 months of each infusion. Univariate and multivariable Cox models and competing risk regression were used to identify factors associated with progression to stage 3b chronic kidney disease (CKD) or worse (eGFR <45 ml min-1 1.73 m-2) in individuals with baseline eGFR ≥45 ml min-1 1.73 m-2.

eGFR declined rapidly in the first year post-transplant (-11.52 ml min-1 1.73 m-2 per year; 95% CI -13.92, -9.00), then stabilised, with decline rates of -3.12 (95% CI -3.84, -2.28) and -1.08 (95% CI -1.80, -0.36) ml min-1 1.73 m-2 per year at 1-5 and 5-20 years, respectively. Female recipients experienced a greater first-year decline than male recipients (-14.79 ml min-1 1.73 m-2 per year [95% CI -17.92, -11.66] vs -6.75 ml min-1 1.73 m-2 per year [95% CI -10.49, -3.01]; p=0.0012). Individuals with baseline eGFR <60 ml min-1 1.73 m-2 had a similar first-year decline compared to those with preserved function (-3.99 ml min-1 1.73 m-2 per year [95% CI -13.31, 5.33] vs -12.03 ml min-1 1.73 m-2 per year [95% CI -14.57, -9.49]; p=0.10). Progression to stage 3b CKD occurred in 21% of participants (47/222) over a median of 6.4 years. Female sex (sub-distribution HR 2.17; 95% CI 1.15, 4.17; p=0.017) and lower baseline eGFR (sub-distribution HR 0.96 per ml min-1 1.73 m-2; 95% CI 0.94, 0.98; p=0.0009) were independent predictors of progression.

Although calcineurin inhibitor-based immunosuppression induces rapid early eGFR decline, its progression slows substantially beyond 5 years. Female sex and lower pre-transplant eGFR independently predicted CKD progression. This sex disparity remains to be fully understood, as male and female recipients did not differ in baseline eGFR or tacrolimus exposure. These findings establish a long-term renal safety benchmark within the largest and longest-running ITA programme, and identify subgroups who are most likely to benefit from emerging calcineurin inhibitor-free strategies.

Article.ArticleTitle: Nonenzymatic Asn Deamidation of GAD65 Generates HLA-DRB1*03:01-Restricted Neoepitopes in Type 1 Diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: GAD65-reactive antibodies are common in individuals with DRB1*03:01 haplotypes and diabetes, and benefits from GAD65 therapy are linked to DRB1*03:01 genotypes. DRB1*03:01 prefers Asp in binding pocket 4, such that Asn deamidation, a modification documented in islets, could generate neoepitopes. DRB1*03:01 should present GAD65 epitopes, but few have been reported. We aimed to identify DRB1*03:01-restricted GAD65 epitopes recognized in individuals with type 1 diabetes (T1D). We defined wild-type and Asn-deamidated GAD65 epitopes that are bound by DRB1*03:01 and assessed their immunogenicity through in vitro T-cell assays. In total, three deamidated and four unmodified GAD65 peptides elicited detectable T-cell responses in individuals with T1D. T-cell clones and lines recognizing each GAD65 epitope were isolated and studied, demonstrating that Asn-deamidated GAD65 epitopes are recognized with higher affinity than unmodified GAD65 epitopes. Furthermore, islet-derived T cells from pancreatic organ donors with T1D recognized Asn-deamidated and unmodified GAD65 epitopes. In total, our work identifies wild-type and deamidated epitopes that drive GAD65-specific T-cell responses in individuals positive for DRB1*03:01. These epitopes can now be applied to characterize GAD65-specific T-cell responses during diabetes progression and in the setting of clinical trials.

DRB1*03:01 is associated with GAD65 autoantibodies and immune modulation with GAD65 protein, but few reliable epitopes have been reported. We aimed to identify relevant GAD65 epitopes recognized in individuals positive for DRB1*03:01. We identified regions of GAD65 that are recognized by CD4+ T cells in individuals with DRB1*03:01 haplotypes and type 1 diabetes, including wild-type and Asn-deamidated epitopes. T cells recognized deamidated GAD65 with higher affinity than wild-type GAD65. GAD65-specific T cells are present among islet-derived T cells from pancreatic organ donors, suggesting a direct role in islet autoimmunity.

Article.ArticleTitle: Continuous Glucose Monitoring- Measured Glucose Levels During Oral Glucose Tolerance Testing in Youths With Obesity: Accuracy and Clinical Implications.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)-derived glucose values versus venous plasma glucose values during oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT) in youths with obesity, their effect on glycemic classification, and whether deconvolution-based reconstruction improves agreement.

Twenty-nine youths with obesity underwent OGTT while wearing a FreeStyle Libre 2 sensor. Raw CGM values were temporally aligned with venous plasma glucose values and used to reconstruct plasma profiles via a first-order plasma-interstitial kinetic model and inverse filtering. Accuracy, agreement, consensus error grid, and glycemic classification were compared with collected venous plasma glucose values.

Temporally aligned CGM-derived values showed limited agreement with collected venous plasma glucose values (mean absolute relative difference [MARD] 12.96%; 51.72% of values within ±10 mg/dL; 20.06% of values differing by >25 mg/dL) and caused classification shifts. After reconstruction, MARD decreased to 5.55%, the proportion of values within ±10 mg/dL increased to 75.86%, almost all values fell within consensus error grid zone A, and classification shifts were reduced.
Deconvolution-based CGM reconstruction may support plasma-referenced, less invasive OGTT-based dysglycemic assessment.
